analysis.one_liner: Raises required gas mileage for cars and SUVs to 40 mpg and 27.5 mpg, and tightens how mileage is tested.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2005 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have gradually forced automakers to build cars that go from a 25 mpg average to 40 mpg, and SUVs, vans, and pickups from 17 mpg to 27.5 mpg, by model years after 2016. It would have counted heavier vehicles like large SUVs under the rules for the first time, doubled fines for violating the mileage rules, fixed the lab tests that overstate real-world gas mileage, and required federal agencies to buy more fuel-efficient vehicles. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save money at the gas pump as new vehicles used less fuel; taxpayers, who fund federal fuel purchases; and the public broadly through reduced oil consumption.

how_it_helps.text: Phases passenger car standards from 25 mpg to 40 mpg for model years after 2016, and light trucks and SUVs from 17 mpg to 27.5 mpg, so new vehicles would use far less gasoline.
Expands the definitions of 'automobile' and 'passenger automobile' to cover vehicles up to 12,000 pounds, closing the loophole that let the heaviest SUVs escape fuel economy rules entirely.
Doubles the civil penalty for violating fuel economy standards from $5 to $10 per tenth of a mile per gallon, with annual inflation adjustments, so violations cost automakers more.

Requires the Volpe Center to study how to make fuel economy tests match real-world driving, then directs the Transportation Secretary to adopt the more accurate test and adjust standards so improved measurement cannot be used to weaken them.

Requires executive agencies to buy or lease vehicles meeting the same mileage standards as everyone else, with at least 20% being exceptionally fuel-efficient and at least 10,000 high-mileage vehicles in the federal fleet by fiscal 2011.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to redesign vehicles to meet much higher mileage requirements, and oil companies, which would sell less gasoline as new cars became more efficient. Some of the automakers' compliance costs could reach buyers through vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs fall on automakers, who argued in this era that steep mileage mandates would force vehicle redesigns and could raise prices or push consumers toward less safe, lighter cars; the bill contains no study of those costs or consumer impacts.
The phase-in ran more than a decade out, to model years after 2016, so most of the fuel savings would not have arrived for years even if the bill had passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fuel savings for drivers and reduced oil dependence are real and substantial, and the bill was carefully built to prevent gaming, including a rule that a more accurate testing procedure could not be used to weaken the standards. The main honest objection is cost: automakers would bear significant redesign expenses, and consumers might see some of that in vehicle prices, though fuel savings over a vehicle's life would likely offset much of it. On balance the benefits to ordinary drivers outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Automobile Fuel Efficiency Improvements Act of 2005 on September 9, 2005.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, who avoided the higher mileage requirements and heavier-vehicle coverage, and oil companies, which kept gasoline demand unchanged. The idea resurfaced in the 2007 energy law, which later raised standards.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it in the Senate.

for.name: 2 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only support beyond the sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ted Stevens (R-AK) in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors were all Democrats and no committee or floor vote was ever held, so there is no record of how either party would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would have forced a steep rise in required fleet mileage and ended the loophole for heavy SUVs, requiring costly redesigns. Its cost is precisely the fuel savings ordinary drivers would have gained.
More efficient vehicles mean less gasoline sold. The industry's interest in weaker standards runs directly against drivers' interest in lower fuel bills.

The bill would have set mileage standards for the federal fleet and required a share of exceptionally efficient vehicles, raising federal procurement standards to match those imposed on private buyers.
